title: Arabic Poetry: Words with Rhythm
summary: How Arabic poetry's rhyme, rhythm, and memory kept history and stories alive long before writing was widespread, and why it is still loved today.
poll: Stories are easier to remember when they are told with rhyme and rhythm.

versions.title: Words That Rhyme
versions.text:
Arab poems are old. People made poems long ago.

A poem is a kind of song in words. It has rhyme. Rhyme is words that end the same. It has rhythm too. Rhythm is a beat you feel.

Long ago, few people could read. Poets did not write poems down. A poet made up a poem in his head. Then he said it out loud. Other people heard it. They would learn it by heart. We call this memorize.

Poems helped people keep stories. Some told of brave deeds. Some told of home. Rhyme and beat made words easy to keep in mind.

Today, people still love these poems. New poets write new poems. Old poems are still loved too.

Today, people still love this old poetry. New poets write new poems, and old poems are still loved too.

versions.title: The Music of Spoken Words
versions.text:
Arab poems are very old, and people across the Arabian Peninsula have made poems for well over a thousand years.

A poem is a kind of song in words. It often has rhyme, words that end the same. It also has rhythm, a beat you can feel. Together, rhyme and rhythm give a poem a musical sound that plain talk does not have.

Long ago, many people could not read or write. Poets did not write their poems down at first. A poet made up a poem in his head, then said it out loud for an audience to hear. Listeners would memorize the poem, learning it by heart, word for word, and then share it with others.

Poems helped whole communities keep stories alive. Some poems told of brave deeds. Some told of family, of generous hosts, and of daily life in the desert. Rhyme and rhythm made these long poems far easier to keep in mind than plain talk would have been.

Today, people across the Arab world still deeply love this old poetry. Poets still write new poems, and old poems are still loved and shared at gatherings today.

versions.title: Poetry Before the Written Page
versions.text:
For well over a thousand years, poetry has held an honored place in Arab culture. It is one of the most respected art forms on the Arabian Peninsula.

A poem is built from rhyme, words that end with the same sound. It is also built from meter, a steady pattern of beats. This gives each line, or verse, a clear rhythm. One important form is the qasida, a long poem built around one meter and one rhyme from the first verse to the last.

Long ago, before writing was common, poets made up their qasidas in their minds. Then they would recite them aloud for an audience. A skilled reciter could hold hundreds of verses in his mind. He could say them with the exact meter and rhyme kept whole. This oral tradition let listeners learn favorite poems and pass them on by word of mouth.

In this way, poetry carried a group's history and stories forward in time, long before most people could read or write. Poems praised courage and kindness, and they kept events alive that might have been lost.

Today, this tradition is still very much alive. Poets still write new poems, and people still gather to hear verses recited at weddings and other events.

versions.title: A Spoken Archive of Memory
versions.text:
For well over a thousand years, poetry has occupied an especially honored place within Arab culture. It functioned as one of the most esteemed art forms on the Arabian Peninsula. This was long before widespread literacy made written composition common across the region.

A poem is constructed from rhyme, words sharing an identical ending sound. It is also constructed from meter, a steady, recurring pattern of beats. This gives each line, or verse, a steady rhythm. One significant traditional form is the qasida, an extended poem built around a single meter and rhyme. It is sustained from the first verse to the last. This demands real eloquence, the skill of speaking gracefully and persuasively.

Before writing became widespread, poets composed their qasidas entirely within their minds through a demanding oral process, memorizing and revising as they went. Then they performed them aloud before an audience. A skilled reciter could memorize hundreds of verses and deliver each with the exact meter and rhyme intact, rarely faltering across a long performance. At gatherings such as the renowned market of Souq Okaz, poets competed publicly, reciting their finest compositions before crowds who judged their artistry and rewarded the most talented among them. Through this oral tradition, listeners memorized favorite poems and faithfully passed them on across generations, preserving them long before manuscripts existed to do so.

In this way, poetry served to preserve a community's history and cherished stories across time. It functioned almost as a spoken archive, built entirely on memory rather than ink. Poems praised courage, generosity, and loyalty, recording events that otherwise might have vanished completely.

Today, this rich heritage remains alive. Poets continue producing new compositions, and audiences still gather to hear verses recited at weddings, celebrations, and competitions held across the wider Arab world today, both large and small.

keyWords.definition: a piece of writing that often uses rhyme and rhythm
keyWords.example: She wrote a poem about the desert sky.

keyWords.definition: words that end with the same sound
keyWords.example: Cat and hat rhyme with each other.

keyWords.definition: a repeating beat that you can feel in words or music
keyWords.example: The drummer kept a steady rhythm during the song.

keyWords.definition: to learn something so well that you can say it without looking
keyWords.example: He had to memorize ten new words for class.

keyWords.definition: a person who writes or recites poems
keyWords.example: The poet read her newest poem to the class.

questions.stem: What is this article mostly about?
options: Why desert winds blow in different directions in the sand and dust
How to build a ship that can sail the Indian Ocean with big sails and strong ropes
Why camels can travel long distances without water in the hot desert sand
How Arabic poetry used rhyme and rhythm to help people remember stories
questions.why: The article explains how rhyme, rhythm, and memory let Arabic poetry pass on stories long ago.

wrong.A: Wind direction is not discussed.
wrong.B: The article does not describe how to build a ship.
wrong.C: Camels are not discussed.

questions.stem: What is rhyme?
options: Words that end with the same sound
A beat you can feel in words and lines
A person who writes poems in a book
A story told only in writing, not by voice
questions.why: The article defines rhyme as words that end with the same sound.

wrong.B: The beat is called rhythm.
wrong.C: A person who writes poems is a poet.
wrong.D: The article says poems were first spoken, not written.

questions.stem: Why didn't poets write their poems down at first?
options: Writing poems down was against the rules
Poems were too long to write down
Many people could not read or write
Poets did not like using paper
questions.why: Many people could not read or write, so poems were not written down at first.

wrong.A: No rule against writing is mentioned.
wrong.B: Poem length is not given as the reason.
wrong.D: A dislike of paper is not mentioned.

questions.stem: In the article, the word memorize means —
options: to write something down neatly
to learn something by heart
to say a poem very loudly
to make up a brand-new poem
questions.why: The article defines memorize as learning something by heart, word for word.

wrong.A: The article says poems were not written down at first.
wrong.C: Loudness is not part of the definition.
wrong.D: Making up a new poem is composing, not memorizing.

questions.stem: Why did rhyme and rhythm make poems easier to remember?
options: They made the poems much shorter and simpler
They were only used by famous poets in books
They made the poems harder to say aloud for children
They gave the words a musical, memorable quality
questions.why: The article says rhyme and rhythm gave the words a musical quality that made them easier to remember.

wrong.A: Length is not linked to rhyme and rhythm.
wrong.B: The article does not limit rhyme to famous poets.
wrong.C: Rhyme and rhythm made poems easier, not harder, to say.

questions.stem: What can you tell about the people who first heard these poems?
options: They had very good memories for words they heard
They preferred written stories over spoken ones
They never shared poems with other people
They disliked stories about brave deeds
questions.why: Listeners could memorize long poems after hearing them only a few times, showing strong memories.

wrong.B: Writing was not widespread, so spoken poems came first.
wrong.C: Listeners passed poems on to others.
wrong.D: Poems about brave deeds were valued, not disliked.

questions.stem: Why did poems often tell about brave deeds and family?
options: Because poets were only allowed to write about weather and the sky
Because these were the only words that rhymed in the language
Because these were things communities valued and wanted remembered
Because poems could not be about daily desert life or its people
questions.why: Poems helped people remember stories about brave deeds and family, showing these mattered to the community.

wrong.A: No such rule is mentioned.
wrong.B: Rhyme is about sound, not subject matter.
wrong.D: Poems also told about daily desert life.

questions.stem: Why does the author end by saying poetry is still loved today?
options: To show that people no longer tell old poems
To show that this tradition has lasted into the present
To explain how to write a brand-new poem for school
To compare poems with other kinds of writing
questions.why: The ending shows that Arabic poetry's tradition continues today, with both new and old poems enjoyed.

wrong.A: The article says old poems are still enjoyed.
wrong.C: No writing instructions are given.
wrong.D: Other kinds of writing are not compared.

LOW.prompt: Imagine you are a poet long ago who cannot write. Explain how you would make your poem easy for others to remember.
checklist: I used the word memorize or poet correctly.
LOW.modelAnswer: As a poet, I would use rhyme, choosing words that end with the same sound, and rhythm, a steady beat in the lines, to make my poem feel musical. This would help listeners memorize my poem quickly, so they could learn it by heart and share it with others after hearing it only a few times.

MID.prompt: Explain how a qasida was composed and recited, and why oral tradition mattered before writing was widespread.
checklist: I explained what a qasida is.
I described how a poem was recited from memory.
I explained why oral tradition was important.
MID.modelAnswer: A qasida is a long poem built around one meter and one rhyme, which a poet composed entirely in his mind before writing was widespread. A skilled reciter would memorize the qasida and recite it aloud to an audience, sometimes at gatherings like Souq Okaz. Oral tradition mattered because it was the main way communities passed on their history and stories at a time when few people could read or write.

HIGH.prompt: Explain how Arabic oral poetry functioned as a 'spoken archive.' Include meter, eloquence, and one way this heritage is preserved today.
checklist: I explained how meter and rhyme supported memory.
I explained what eloquence means and why it mattered.
I described how this heritage is preserved or valued today.
HIGH.modelAnswer: Arabic oral poetry worked as a spoken archive because meter and rhyme gave each verse a steady, memorable rhythm that reciters could preserve across generations without writing. Eloquence, the skill of expressing ideas gracefully and persuasively, mattered deeply because audiences judged and rewarded the most talented poets at gatherings like Souq Okaz. Today, this heritage lives on as poets continue composing new works and audiences still gather to hear verses recited at weddings and celebrations.
